slides.title: Get started
slides.html:
Converse check: students write the converse of Theorem 9 and vote on whether it is true just because Theorem 9 is. Then they flip a paper triangle over onto itself.

  • I can prove the converse of Theorem 9 (Theorem 10) by comparing the triangle with itself using ASA.
  • I can explain why equilateral and equiangular mean the same thing for triangles, with no 60 degree value yet.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.html: the converse needs its own proof. The self-comparison trick: triangle ABC and triangle ACB.

geo.title: The big idea
geo.body: the converse needs its own proof. The self-comparison trick: triangle ABC and triangle ACB.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Proof of Theorem 10 (adapted from Jacobs p. 159).

Read the worked steps
StepReason
In triangle ABC, angle B ≅ angle C.Given.
Compare triangle ABC with triangle ACB, the same triangle read in a different order.The self-comparison trick.
Angle ABC ≅ angle ACB and angle ACB ≅ angle ABC.Given, read both ways.
BC = CB.A segment equals itself.
Triangle ABC ≅ triangle ACB.ASA.
AB = AC.CPCTC. No AAS and no angle sum needed.

steps.step: In triangle ABC, angle B ≅ angle C.

slides.title: Worked example
slides.html:
Equal angles give equal sides (original).

Read the worked steps
StepReason
Angle A = angle B = angle C.Given.
AB = AC = BC.Theorem 10, used on two pairs of angles.
AB = 2x + 1 and BC = 9, so 2x + 1 = 9 and x = 4.Solve.
Every side is 9.Substitute.
Going the other way, equal sides give equal angles.Theorem 9. We still don't name a number of degrees.

slides.title: Common mistake
slides.html:
Jordan says reversing a true theorem proves its converse.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Find and fix the error

Flipping the if and then does not prove the converse. Theorem 10 needs its own proof (the ASA self-comparison).

geo.title: Common mistake
geo.prompt: Jordan says reversing a true theorem proves its converse.
geo.correction: Flipping the if and then does not prove the converse. Theorem 10 needs its own proof (the ASA self-comparison).

slides.title: Practice 1
slides.html:
In triangle PQR, angle P = angle Q. Which sides are equal?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

QR = PR, the sides across from those angles.

Reveal second check

The side across from P doesn't use the letter P, and the same for Q.

slides.title: Practice 2
slides.html:
Angle B = angle C, AB = 5x - 4, AC = 2x + 11. Find x.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

5x - 4 = 2x + 11, so 3x = 15 and x = 5. Both sides are 21.

Reveal second check

25 - 4 = 21 and 10 + 11 = 21.

geo.title: Practice 2

geo.solution: 5x - 4 = 2x + 11, so 3x = 15 and x = 5. Both sides are 21.

slides.title: Practice 3
slides.html:
Why does equilateral mean equiangular?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Use Theorem 9 on two different pairs of equal sides.

Reveal second check

That gives A = B and B = C, so all three are equal.

geo.title: Practice 3
geo.solution: Use Theorem 9 on two different pairs of equal sides.
geo.check: That gives A = B and B = C, so all three are equal.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.html:
Why is every equilateral triangle equiangular?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Apply the Isosceles Triangle Theorem to each pair of equal sides: each pair of angles opposite them is equal, so all three angles are equal.

Reveal second check

Name the givens and the theorem or definition used.

geo.title: Check yourself
geo.prompt: Why is every equilateral triangle equiangular?
geo.solution: Apply the Isosceles Triangle Theorem to each pair of equal sides: each pair of angles opposite them is equal, so all three angles are equal.
